zh.title: 美國為何擔心加拿大與歐洲的戰機製造談判：F-35、獅鷲與北美防空司令部的角力
zh.summary: 加拿大計畫採購88架F-35A、目前僅簽約16架，首兩架已於2026年10月交付；是否削減訂單並引進瑞典獅鷲戰機，引發美國對北美防空司令部互通性的擔憂。爭議核心不是價格或性能，而是主權、控制權與地緣政治。
body: 美國是否擔心加拿大在加拿大製造瑞典紳寶JAS 39獅鷲戰機？某種程度上是，但真正的擔憂不在獅鷲本身。加拿大以88架F-35A汰換老舊的CF-18機隊為既定計畫，目前簽約採購16架，首兩架已於2026年10月交付，現留駐亞利桑那州路克空軍基地供訓練使用；當前的討論不是取消F-35，而是把訂單由88架縮減、改為同時操作兩種戰機，類似英國、澳洲與義大利空軍的做法。獅鷲與北約Link 16、北約武器與西方感測器相容，卻未獲北美防空司令部（NORAD）認證；加拿大於2022年拒絕獅鷲，部分原因是評估認為它足以應付基本任務，卻不足以滿足北美防空司令部的完整需求。紳寶表示可以讓獅鷲符合北美防空司令部標準，但尚未說明如何做到。

北美防空司令部是爭議的核心。戰機不只是戰機，更是龐大體系的節點：美國與北約盟國共享Link 16，但北美防空司令部不是北約；北美防空司令部飛機必須使用美國控制的IFF Mode 5、飛彈防禦資料鏈，以及與美國預警系統連結的機密資料鏈。F-35以美國控制的專屬軟體與生態系設計，能整合進北美防空司令部的指揮管制基礎設施；美國駐加拿大大使皮特·胡克斯特拉（Pete Hoekstra）稱獅鷲為次等產品、互通性不如F-35。加拿大方面則擔心主權：F-35雖是性能最強的戰機，卻讓國家最頂尖的防衛能力依賴美國技術與後勤，甚至引發終止開關（kill-switch）的疑慮。據加拿大廣播公司引述的國防部外洩評估，F-35軍事能力得分95%（60分中得57.1分），獅鷲E僅33%（19.8分）；加拿大全球事務研究所所長大衛·裴利（David Perry）認為評估結果顯示勝負毫無懸念。

成本與性能的爭論多半是煙幕。獅鷲E的成本超支據Defense Express估計相當於八架戰機的造價，紳寶向巴西交付獅鷲E的進度落後達八年；芬蘭於2021年在分散式空軍作戰想定下選擇F-35A而非獅鷲。達梭於2018年退出加拿大競標、歐洲戰機隨後於2019年跟進，空中巴士表示北美防空司令部安全要求對製造與維修鏈位於美加雙眼（2-EYES）社群之外的平台成本過高。獅鷲E使用奇異航太發動機，同樣受美國出口管制，反而削弱加拿大追求的主權。哥倫比亞前任政府曾簽約採購獅鷲，親美反對派贏得總統大選後改為尋求重新談判；秘魯則已取消獅鷲採購、改選F-16。對美國而言，加拿大採購獅鷲本身並無不可，條件是同時採購足夠的F-35以確實執行北美防空司令部任務。

en.title: Why the US is worried about Canada and Europe's aircraft manufacturing talks: F-35, Gripen and NORAD
en.summary: Canada plans to buy 88 F-35As and has contracted 16, with the first two delivered in October 2026; whether it cuts the order and adds Sweden's Gripen has Washington worried about NORAD interoperability. The core of the debate is sovereignty, control and geopolitics — not price or performance.
body: Is the United States worried about Canada building Swedish Saab JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets in Canada? Sort of — but the real worry is not the Gripen itself. Canada selected the F-35A to replace its aging CF-18 Hornets with a program of record for 88 aircraft, of which it is currently contracted to purchase 16 examples; the first two were delivered in October 2026 and are being kept at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona for training. The current discourse is not so much about Canada canceling the F-35 entirely — those 16 aircraft are already contracted — as about reducing the order from 88 jets and operating two types of fighter jets, something similar to the Royal Air Force, the Royal Australian Air Force and the Italian Air Force. The Gripen is NATO-compatible with Link 16, NATO weapons and Western sensors, but it is not certified to be integrated into NORAD; Canada rejected the Gripen in 2022, partly because, as it assessed, the Gripen was sufficient for basic tasks but insufficient for full NORAD demands. Saab has said it can make the Gripen NORAD-compliant, but has not been able to show how it can do this.

At the heart of the issue from the American perspective is NORAD. Fighter jets are nodes of a major, more comprehensive and powerful system: the United States shares Link 16 with its other NATO allies, but NORAD is not NATO. A NORAD aircraft must use US-controlled IFF Mode 5, missile defense data links, classified datalinks tied to US early warning, and more. The F-35 has been designed with proprietary US-controlled software and an ecosystem built to integrate with NORAD's C2 infrastructure. US Ambassador Pete Hoekstra has called the Gripen an "inferior product" and one that's "not as interchangeable." From Canada's point of view, the F-35 may be the most capable fighter jet by a long shot, but that is undermined by the fear of a "kill-switch" and having the country's top defensive capabilities dependent on US technology and sustainment. To quote Radio Canada reporting on a Canadian Department of National Defense leak, "the F-35 got a score of 95% on military capabilities, with a total of 57.1 points out of 60. By contrast, the Gripen-E finished with a score of 33%, netting 19.8 points out of 60." David Perry, president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, said: "The capability assessment here says that there is a clear-cut winner, no contest, no ambiguity. I'd expected that [the F-35] was going to be a clear winner, but this is a winner by a mile."

Debates over costs and capabilities are largely distractions from the real issues, which are geopolitical. Saab is up to eight years behind delivering the Gripen E to Brazil, while cost overruns are "equal to eight fighter jets," according to Defense Express. Finland uses its fighter jets in a dispersed doctrine similar to Sweden, and in 2021 it selected the F-35A as the best aircraft to continue that doctrine over the Gripen. Dassault Aviation pulled its Rafale fighter jet out of Canada's CF-18 replacement competition in 2018, and the Eurofighter followed in 2019, with Airbus saying that "NORAD security requirements continue to place too significant a cost on platforms whose manufacture and repair chains sit outside the United States-Canada 2-EYES community." The Gripen E has a GE Aerospace engine and is very much subject to US export controls, paradoxically eating into Canada's sovereignty requirement. Colombia's previous US-skeptical government signed for the Gripen, while the pro-US opposition has since won the presidency and has so far looked at renegotiating the deal rather than canceling it; Peru has canceled the Gripen, instead opting for the F-16. For the US, Canada purchasing the Gripen is fine if it also purchases enough F-35s to confidently carry out its NORAD missions.
